content: The central venous catheter (CVC) is a medical device used for various purposes, including monitoring hemodynamic parameters, administering intravenous medications, fluids, blood products, and parenteral nutrition. However, as a foreign object introduced into the body, it is prone to colonization by microorganisms. This colonization can lead to catheter-related bloodstream infections (BSIs), which are associated with increased mortality, morbidity, and healthcare costs. The objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of skin antisepsis as part of CVC care on reducing catheter-related BSIs, catheter colonization, and patient mortality and morbidity. A comprehensive search was conducted in May 2016 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Wounds Specialised Register, CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, and EBSCO CINAHL Plus. Clinical trial registries were also searched for ongoing and unpublished studies. No restrictions were applied regarding language, publication date, or study setting. The study included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated any type of skin antiseptic agent, either used alone or in combination, compared to other antiseptic agents, placebo, or no antisepsis in patients with a CVC. Two authors independently assessed the eligibility of studies, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias. Results were expressed using risk ratios (RR), absolute risk reduction (ARR), and the number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome (NNTB) for dichotomous data, as well as mean differences (MD) for continuous data, all with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Thirteen studies met the inclusion criteria, but only 12 contributed data, involving a total of 3446 CVCs. The total number of participants was unclear due to incomplete reporting in some studies. Most participants were adults admitted to intensive care units, hematology-oncology units, or general wards. Skin antisepsis was typically performed prior to catheter insertion and regularly during the indwelling period, with intervals ranging from 24 to 72 hours. The methodological quality of the studies varied, with many showing a high risk of bias due to inadequate blinding and incomplete outcome data. Three studies compared different antiseptic regimens to no antisepsis. These comparisons did not demonstrate clear evidence of differences in outcomes such as catheter-related BSI, septicemia, catheter colonization, or the need for systemic antibiotics. However, the analyses were underpowered, and the overall quality of evidence was very low, leading to significant uncertainty in the findings. Head-to-head comparisons between different antiseptic agents were also conducted, with the most frequent comparison being chlorhexidine versus povidone-iodine. There was very low-quality evidence suggesting that chlorhexidine may reduce catheter-related BSIs compared to povidone-iodine (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.99; ARR 2.30%, 95% CI 0.06% to 3.70%). This evidence was derived from four studies involving 1436 catheters. Subgroup analyses comparing aqueous chlorhexidine to aqueous povidone-iodine, alcoholic chlorhexidine to aqueous povidone-iodine, and alcoholic chlorhexidine to alcoholic povidone-iodine did not show clear differences in catheter-related BSIs or mortality, and these analyses were generally underpowered. Mortality was reported in only one study. There was also very low-quality evidence indicating that chlorhexidine may reduce catheter colonization compared to povidone-iodine (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.84; ARR 8%, 95% CI 3% to 12%). This finding was based on five studies involving 1533 catheters, but the evidence was downgraded due to risk of bias, indirectness, and inconsistency. Other antiseptic agents were evaluated in single, small studies, many of which did not report the primary outcome of catheter-related BSI. Additionally, outcomes such as skin infections and adverse events were poorly reported across trials. In conclusion, it remains unclear whether skin antisepsis around CVC insertion sites reduces catheter-related BSIs compared to no antisepsis. There is very low-quality evidence suggesting that chlorhexidine may reduce rates of catheter-related BSIs and catheter colonization compared to povidone-iodine. However, the true effects may differ significantly due to the low quality of evidence and potential influence of the antiseptic solution's formulation (aqueous or alcohol-based). Further high-quality RCTs are needed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of different skin antisepsis regimens in CVC care, with a focus on critical clinical outcomes such as sepsis, catheter-related BSIs, and mortality.
